newsitem.title: USA: Vaccine created for urinary tract infection - study.
newsitem.headline: Vaccine created for urinary tract infection - study.

text.p: A new vaccine that blocks urinary tract infections in mice could help prevent the ailment in humans and might be applied to other diseases caused by bacteria, scientists said on Thursday.

The vaccine was developed by isolating the sticky proteins that allow bacteria to adhere to the bladder wall and then injecting a form of those proteins into laboratory mice, whose bodies formed antibodies to fight the infection.

As many as 50 percent of American women suffer urinary tract infections including bladder infections and cystitis at some time in their lives. Such infections account for millions of visits to doctors and cost more than $1 billion each year in the United States, the researchers said.

The disease, usually caused by E. coli bacteria, affects mostly women and causes symptoms including pain and itching. Such infections are treated with antibiotics but the ailment often recurs, said Scott Hultgren, a molecular biologist at Washington University in St. Louis, who worked on the study, reported in the latest edition of the journal Science.

Hultgren said by telephone that researchers had managed to find a "molecular machine" in bacteria that produces hairlike fibers called pili that are the glue that binds E. coli to the bladder. He said this technique could be used to fight other bacteria-caused diseases including middle-ear infections, pneumonia, meningitis, kidney infections and gonorrhea.
Researchers at the private biotechnology firm MedImmune Inc., based in Gaithersburg, Maryland, and the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden, also worked on the study.

MedImmune's Solomon Langermann, lead author of the Science article, said in a statement: "Our discoveries represent significant progress towards a novel vaccination strategy which has initially shown promise for UTIs (urinary tract infections) and may be applicable for combating other bacterial diseases as well."

The company is testing its candidate vaccine in monkeys and plans to seek approval for human clinical trials beginning next year. While the path from laboratory research on animals to a vaccine for humans can vary in length, it said the three phases of clinical study required for drug approval by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration can take from four to six years.
